```{r}
#| label: Setup
#| include: false
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)

source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/format_path.R?raw=true")
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_llmpanel.R"))

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")
raw_panel <- read_csv(here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

tone_levels <- c("norms", "acknowledging", "legitimizing",
                 "self_efficacy", "value_affirmation")
pref_cols <- paste0("pref_", tone_levels)
order_levels <- c("Preferences first", "Messages first")

set.seed(102030)
n_boot <- 1000   # the reliability bootstrap takes a minute or two

# Survey order. `tone_order` and `message_order` are the positions (1 or 2) of the
# preferences survey and the message-rating survey. format_eda() drops them, so
# they are taken from the raw panel and joined by subid.
survey_order <- raw_panel |>
  transmute(subid, tone_order, message_order, survey_version,
            block_order_hi, block_order_hd, block_order_li,
            pref_order = factor(
              case_when(tone_order < message_order ~ "Preferences first",
                        tone_order > message_order ~ "Messages first"),
              levels = order_levels))

panel <- format_eda(raw_panel) |>
  left_join(survey_order |> select(subid, pref_order), by = "subid")

panel_long <- format_eda(raw_panel, long = TRUE) |>
  left_join(survey_order |> select(subid, pref_order), by = "subid")

# Respondent-level summaries
rating_by_tone <- panel_long |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, pref_order, tone))

pref_by_tone <- panel |>
  select(subid, pref_order, all_of(pref_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(pref_cols), names_to = "tone", names_prefix = "pref_",
               values_to = "pref")

respondent <- panel_long |>
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_rating = sd(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_distinct_ratings = n_distinct(rating_num),
            .by = c(subid, pref_order)) |>
  left_join(pref_by_tone |>
              summarise(mean_pref = mean(pref, na.rm = TRUE),
                        sd_pref = sd(pref, na.rm = TRUE), .by = subid),
            by = "subid") |>
  mutate(pref_straightline = sd_pref == 0)

# Difference between orders (Messages first minus Preferences first) with a
# Welch t-test, as one row
order_test <- function(data, col, label) {
  x <- data[[col]][data$pref_order == "Messages first"]
  y <- data[[col]][data$pref_order == "Preferences first"]
  tt <- t.test(x, y)
  tibble(measure = label,
         prefs_first = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
         messages_first = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         diff = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
         ci_low = tt$conf.int[1], ci_high = tt$conf.int[2],
         d = diff / sd(c(x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), y - mean(y, na.rm = TRUE)), na.rm = TRUE),
         p = tt$p.value)
}

fmt_p <- \(p) if_else(p < .001, "< .001", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
```

**Code status:** runs. The written conclusions below describe the render of
2026-11-16 (n = 424). If the data or exclusions change, re-check them against
the tables.

# Question

Respondents completed two surveys in random order: the **preferences survey**
(how much they like each tone in the abstract, plus formality) and the
**message ratings** (30 example messages). The preregistered secondary aim
asks whether stated preferences are a better guide to message ratings when
they are collected before or after people have seen example messages. This
memo also checks whether order changed the ratings themselves.

Four questions, in order:

1.  Were the two order groups comparable?
2.  Did order change the **message ratings** (their level or their reliability)?
3.  Did order change the **stated preferences**?
4.  Did order change how well **preferences predict ratings**?

# At a Glance

```{r}
#| label: Placeholder for summary
# The summary table is printed at the end of the document (Section 5), after
# every test has been run. Copy the conclusions here once reviewed.
```

**Survey order made no robust difference to how well a person's stated
preferences match their own ratings across tones.** The within-person correlation between preferences
and ratings was the same in both orders (0.28 vs. 0.30, p = .66). The
unstandardized slope was steeper when preferences came first (0.23 vs. 0.17,
p = .022), but that difference does not survive adjustment for the number of
tests (Holm p = .22) and is partly a matter of scale (see Section 4).

Order did change how people used the scales:

-   **Message ratings.** The level was unchanged (5.15 vs. 5.23, p = .34).
    Respondents who saw the tone descriptions first discriminated more between
    messages (within-person SD 1.07 vs. 0.94, p = .002). This is the only
    difference that survives adjustment (Holm p = .020).
-   **Stated preferences.** After rating 30 messages, people straightlined
    their preferences less (9.5% vs. 16.8%, p = .035) and their preferences
    moved toward what they had just rated: acknowledging down 0.30, value
    affirmation up 0.22 (tone by order p = .004).

**The registered model-based test finds a difference, and it is about overall
level, not the match between tones.** Fit separately in each half, the
preferences model predicted ratings better when messages came first (R² 0.24
vs. 0.11, p = .002; `prereg_models_glmnet.qmd`). Section 4 shows why. People
who stated higher preferences overall also rated messages higher overall, and
that link was stronger when messages came first (r = 0.70 vs. 0.51, p = .002).
A person's overall preference level explained 21% of rating variance in that
order against 10% when preferences came first. The tone-specific part of
preferences explained 2% against 3%, no better when messages came first.

For deployment, preferences have to be collected at onboarding, before any
message is seen. The tone-specific match that assignment relies on was no
weaker in that order.

# 1. The Two Groups

```{r}
#| label: Order check
# The two position variables should always be 1 and 2 in some order
survey_order |> count(tone_order, message_order, pref_order)
```

If any row above has a missing `pref_order`, or positions that are not one 1
and one 2, stop: the order variable is not what this memo assumes.

```{r}
#| label: Group sizes
panel |> count(pref_order) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

# Order by message set (survey version) should be roughly balanced
survey_order |> count(survey_version, pref_order) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pref_order, values_from = n)
chisq.test(table(survey_order$survey_version, survey_order$pref_order))
```

**Balance on demographics.** Order was randomized, so the groups should not
differ. Numeric variables use a Welch t-test and categorical variables a
chi-square test.

```{r}
#| label: Balance
dem_vars <- str_subset(names(panel), "^dem_") |> setdiff("dem_income")

balance <- map(dem_vars, \(v) {
  x <- panel[[v]]
  g <- panel$pref_order
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    tibble(variable = v, test = "Welch t",
           prefs_first = as.character(round(mean(x[g == order_levels[1]], na.rm = TRUE), 2)),
           messages_first = as.character(round(mean(x[g == order_levels[2]], na.rm = TRUE), 2)),
           p = t.test(x ~ g)$p.value)
  } else {
    tibble(variable = v, test = "Chi-square",
           prefs_first = "", messages_first = "",
           p = suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table(x, g))$p.value))
  }
}) |> list_rbind() |>
  arrange(p)
balance
```

# 2. Did Order Change the Message Ratings?

## Level and spread of ratings

Each respondent's mean rating across their 30 messages, the SD of their 30
ratings (how much they discriminated between messages), and how many distinct
scale points they used.

```{r}
#| label: Rating level
rating_tests <- bind_rows(
  order_test(respondent, "mean_rating", "Mean message rating"),
  order_test(respondent, "sd_rating", "Within-person SD of ratings"),
  order_test(respondent, "n_distinct_ratings", "Distinct scale points used"))
rating_tests |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !p, \(x) round(x, 3)), p = fmt_p(p))
```

```{r}
#| label: Rating level plot
respondent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pref_order, y = mean_rating, fill = pref_order)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Respondent's mean message rating")
```

## Ratings by tone

Did seeing the tone descriptions first change which tones were rated higher?
The `pref_order:tone` row is the test.

```{r}
#| label: Tone by order
rating_by_tone |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), .by = c(pref_order, tone)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pref_order, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(diff = `Messages first` - `Preferences first`) |>
  arrange(desc(`Preferences first`))

aov_rating <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "subid", dv = "rating",
  data = rating_by_tone |> mutate(subid = factor(subid)),
  within = "tone", between = "pref_order",
  anova_table = list(correction = "GG", es = "pes"))
aov_rating
```

```{r}
#| label: Tone by order plot
rating_by_tone |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), se = sd(rating) / sqrt(n()), .by = c(pref_order, tone)) |>
  mutate(tone = fct_reorder(str_to_sentence(str_replace(tone, "_", " ")), mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tone, y = mean, color = pref_order, group = pref_order)) +
  geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean message rating", color = NULL)
```

## Reliability of ratings

Two kinds of reliability, each computed within order group:

-   **Overall level.** Does a person who rates messages high in one risk
    context rate them high in the others? Cronbach's alpha across the three
    context means.
-   **Tone profile.** Does a person's pattern across the five tones repeat
    from one context to another? The correlation between contexts of each
    person's individual tone profile (their rating of a tone, relative to
    their own average and to the sample's average for that tone), projected to
    three contexts with Spearman-Brown.

Intervals and the test of the difference come from a respondent-level
bootstrap within each group.

```{r}
#| label: Reliability
context_means <- panel_long |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, pref_order, context, tone))
contexts <- sort(unique(context_means$context))

# One row per respondent: their 3 context means, and their individual tone
# profile in each context (15 values)
level_wide <- context_means |>
  summarise(level = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, pref_order, context)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = context, values_from = level, names_prefix = "level_")

reliability_stats <- function(subids) {
  # `subids` may contain repeats (bootstrap); each draw is treated as a new person
  draws <- tibble(subid = subids, draw = seq_along(subids))

  lv <- draws |> inner_join(level_wide, by = "subid") |>
    select(starts_with("level_")) |> drop_na()
  k <- ncol(lv)
  alpha <- k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(lv, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(lv)))

  prof <- draws |>
    inner_join(context_means, by = "subid", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(dev = rating - mean(rating), .by = c(draw, context)) |>
    mutate(dev = dev - mean(dev), .by = c(context, tone)) |>
    select(draw, tone, context, dev) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = context, values_from = dev)
  r <- mean(map_dbl(combn(contexts, 2, simplify = FALSE),
                    \(p) cor(prof[[p[1]]], prof[[p[2]]], use = "complete.obs")))

  c(alpha_level = alpha, r_profile = r, rel3_profile = 3 * r / (1 + 2 * r))
}

group_ids <- split(respondent$subid, respondent$pref_order)
observed <- map(group_ids, reliability_stats)

boot <- map(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) {
  map(group_ids, \(g) reliability_stats(sample(g, replace = TRUE)))
})

reliability_table <- map(names(observed[[1]]), \(stat) {
  b1 <- map_dbl(boot, \(b) b[[order_levels[1]]][[stat]])
  b2 <- map_dbl(boot, \(b) b[[order_levels[2]]][[stat]])
  tibble(
    measure = stat,
    prefs_first = observed[[order_levels[1]]][[stat]],
    messages_first = observed[[order_levels[2]]][[stat]],
    diff = messages_first - prefs_first,
    ci_low = quantile(b2 - b1, .025),
    ci_high = quantile(b2 - b1, .975),
    # two-sided bootstrap p-value for a difference of zero
    p = min(1, 2 * min(mean(b2 - b1 <= 0), mean(b2 - b1 >= 0))))
}) |> list_rbind() |>
  mutate(measure = case_when(
    measure == "alpha_level" ~ "Overall level: alpha across 3 contexts",
    measure == "r_profile" ~ "Tone profile: correlation between contexts",
    measure == "rel3_profile" ~ "Tone profile: reliability over 3 contexts"))
reliability_table |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !p, \(x) round(x, 3)), p = fmt_p(p))
```

Reading the first render: overall-level reliability was high in both orders
(alpha 0.91 vs. 0.93). Tone-profile reliability was somewhat higher when
preferences came first (0.63 vs. 0.52), but the difference was not significant
(p = .07). Seeing the tone descriptions first may sharpen how people
distinguish tones; the evidence is suggestive only.

# 3. Did Order Change the Stated Preferences?

Respondents who rated 30 messages first had concrete examples in mind when
they stated their preferences. Did they report different preferences, or
discriminate more between tones?

```{r}
#| label: Preference level
pref_tests <- bind_rows(
  order_test(respondent, "mean_pref", "Mean tone preference"),
  order_test(respondent, "sd_pref", "Within-person SD of tone preferences"),
  order_test(panel |> mutate(pref_formality = as.numeric(pref_formality)),
             "pref_formality", "Formality preference (1 informal - 6 formal)"))
pref_tests |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !p, \(x) round(x, 3)), p = fmt_p(p))

# Preference straightlining (same score for all five tones)
straight_table <- table(respondent$pref_order, respondent$pref_straightline)
straight_table
prop.table(straight_table, 1)
straight_test <- chisq.test(straight_table)
straight_test
```

```{r}
#| label: Preference by tone
pref_by_tone |>
  summarise(mean = mean(pref, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(pref_order, tone)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pref_order, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(diff = `Messages first` - `Preferences first`) |>
  arrange(desc(`Preferences first`))

aov_pref <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "subid", dv = "pref",
  data = pref_by_tone |> drop_na(pref) |> mutate(subid = factor(subid)),
  within = "tone", between = "pref_order",
  anova_table = list(correction = "GG", es = "pes"))
aov_pref
```

# 4. Did Order Change How Well Preferences Predict Ratings?

This is the preregistered secondary aim. The preregistration planned to
compare the preferences model's cross-validated performance between the two
halves of the sample. The tests here are a simpler, direct version of the same
question and should be described as such.

## Within-person agreement

For each respondent, the correlation across the five tones between their
stated preference and their mean message rating. A respondent whose ratings
follow their stated preferences has a high correlation. It is undefined for
respondents with no variation in their preferences or in their tone ratings,
who are counted separately.

```{r}
#| label: Within-person agreement
agreement <- pref_by_tone |>
  inner_join(rating_by_tone |> select(subid, tone, rating), by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(r = if (sd(pref) > 0 && sd(rating) > 0) cor(pref, rating) else NA_real_,
            .by = c(subid, pref_order))

agreement |>
  summarise(n = n(), undefined = sum(is.na(r)),
            mean_r = mean(r, na.rm = TRUE), median_r = median(r, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_positive = mean(r > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = pref_order)

agreement_test <- order_test(drop_na(agreement, r), "r",
                             "Within-person preference-rating correlation")
agreement_test |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !p, \(x) round(x, 3)), p = fmt_p(p))
wilcox.test(r ~ pref_order, data = agreement)
```

```{r}
#| label: Agreement plot
agreement |>
  drop_na(r) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = r, fill = pref_order)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0, color = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~pref_order, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Correlation between stated preference and mean rating, across the five tones",
       y = "Respondents")
```

## Mixed model

All 30 ratings per respondent. `pref_dev` is the respondent's preference for
the message's tone minus their own mean preference, so its slope is the rise
in rating for each point a tone is preferred above the person's average.

-   `pref_dev:pref_order` tests whether that slope differs by survey order
    (the secondary aim).
-   The three-way term tests whether the order effect on the slope differs by
    tone.

```{r}
#| label: Mixed model
model_data <- panel_long |>
  left_join(pref_by_tone |> select(subid, tone, pref_own = pref), by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  mutate(pref_mean = mean(pref_own, na.rm = TRUE), .by = subid) |>
  mutate(pref_dev = pref_own - pref_mean,
         subid = factor(subid),
         tone = factor(tone, levels = tone_levels),
         style = factor(style),
         context = factor(context)) |>
  drop_na(rating_num, pref_dev, pref_order)

m_base <- lme4::lmer(
  rating_num ~ tone * pref_dev + pref_order + pref_mean + style + context +
    (1 | subid) + (1 | subid:tone),
  data = model_data, REML = FALSE)
m_order <- update(m_base, . ~ . + pref_dev:pref_order)
m_order_tone <- update(m_order, . ~ . + tone:pref_order + tone:pref_dev:pref_order)

lrt_order <- anova(m_base, m_order)
lrt_order
lrt_order_tone <- anova(m_order, m_order_tone)
lrt_order_tone

# Preference slope within each order (averaged over tones)
slopes_order <- emmeans::emtrends(m_order, ~ pref_order, var = "pref_dev",
                                  lmer.df = "asymptotic")
slopes_order
slope_contrast <- pairs(slopes_order) |> confint() |> as_tibble()
slope_contrast

# Preference slope for each tone within each order
slopes_order_tone <- emmeans::emtrends(m_order_tone, ~ pref_order | tone, var = "pref_dev",
                                       lmer.df = "asymptotic")
slopes_order_tone
```

```{r}
#| label: Slope plot
as_tibble(slopes_order_tone) |>
  mutate(tone = str_to_sentence(str_replace(as.character(tone), "_", " "))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pref_dev.trend, y = tone, color = pref_order)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = asymp.LCL, xmax = asymp.UCL),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Change in message rating per 1-point higher preference for that tone",
       y = NULL, color = NULL)
```

Reading the first render: the two analyses disagree. The correlation shows no
order effect; the slope is steeper when preferences come first. A slope is
unstandardized, and the messages-first group spread their preferences more
(SD 0.88 vs. 0.77) and their ratings less (SD 0.94 vs. 1.07). Both shifts
flatten a slope without changing the correlation, so the slope difference
should not be read as preferences being more accurate when collected first.

The order effect on the slope differed by tone (p = .003). The norms slope was
0.43 when preferences came first and 0.24 when they came second; legitimizing
went from 0.16 to 0.04; value affirmation and self efficacy moved the other
way. These tone-level differences are exploratory.

## Overall level versus tone-specific match

The registered version of this test (in `prereg_models_glmnet.qmd`) fits the
preferences model separately in each half. It predicted ratings better when
messages came first (R² 0.24 vs. 0.11; relative error 0.86 vs. 0.95,
p = .002). The within-person agreement above did not differ. This section
checks one explanation for the disagreement: that preferences stated after
rating the messages track a person's *overall* rating level more closely,
which helps a model predict ratings without telling it which tone suits whom.

A stated preference is split into two parts: the person's mean preference
across the five tones (`pref_mean`, their overall level) and how far each tone
sits above or below that mean (`pref_dev`, the tone-specific part).

**Do people who state higher preferences overall also rate messages higher
overall?**

```{r}
#| label: Level correlation
level_cor <- respondent |>
  drop_na(mean_pref, mean_rating) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            r = cor(mean_pref, mean_rating),
            rho = cor(mean_pref, mean_rating, method = "spearman"),
            .by = pref_order) |>
  arrange(pref_order) |>
  mutate(ci_low = tanh(atanh(r) - 1.96 / sqrt(n - 3)),
         ci_high = tanh(atanh(r) + 1.96 / sqrt(n - 3)))
level_cor |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !n, \(x) round(x, 3)))

# Difference between the two independent correlations (Fisher z)
level_z <- diff(atanh(level_cor$r)) / sqrt(sum(1 / (level_cor$n - 3)))
tibble(comparison = "Messages first minus Preferences first",
       diff_r = diff(level_cor$r), z = level_z,
       p = fmt_p(2 * pnorm(-abs(level_z)))) |>
  mutate(across(c(diff_r, z), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: Level correlation plot
respondent |>
  drop_na(mean_pref, mean_rating) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_pref, mean_rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ pref_order) +
  labs(x = "Mean stated preference (five tones)",
       y = "Mean message rating (30 messages)")
```

**How much of the rating variance does each part of the preferences explain?**
Variance in individual ratings explained (R²) by linear models fit within each
order. Every model includes tone, style and context. These are in-sample
values with few predictors, so they are comparable across orders but are not
the cross-validated figures from the registered models.

```{r}
#| label: Variance explained by part
r2_parts <- map(order_levels, \(g) {
  d <- filter(model_data, pref_order == g)
  r2 <- \(f) summary(lm(f, data = d))$r.squared
  tibble(pref_order = g,
         design_only = r2(rating_num ~ tone + style + context),
         plus_level = r2(rating_num ~ tone + style + context + pref_mean),
         plus_tone_specific = r2(rating_num ~ tone * pref_dev + style + context),
         plus_both = r2(rating_num ~ tone * pref_dev + style + context + pref_mean))
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(gain_level = plus_level - design_only,
         gain_tone_specific = plus_tone_specific - design_only)
r2_parts |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

**Is there simply more between-person variance to explain in one half?** The
share of rating variance that lies between people (the most any person-level
predictor could explain), and the slope of mean rating on mean preference.

```{r}
#| label: Between-person share
map(order_levels, \(g) {
  d <- filter(model_data, pref_order == g)
  r <- filter(respondent, pref_order == g) |> drop_na(mean_pref, mean_rating)
  tibble(pref_order = g,
         var_rating = var(d$rating_num),
         between_person_share = var(r$mean_rating) / var(d$rating_num),
         sd_mean_pref = sd(r$mean_pref),
         slope_level = coef(lm(mean_rating ~ mean_pref, data = r))[["mean_pref"]])
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# Does the level slope differ by order?
lm(mean_rating ~ mean_pref * pref_order, data = respondent) |>
  summary() |> coef() |> round(3)
```

**How to read this.** If the explanation holds, the level correlation and
`gain_level` are clearly larger when messages came first, while
`gain_tone_specific` is similar in the two orders. Assignment depends only on
the tone-specific part, so in that case the registered result does not weaken
the case for collecting preferences at onboarding. If `gain_tone_specific` is
also larger when messages came first, preferences collected at onboarding are
a weaker guide to assignment than the within-person correlation suggests.

# 5. Summary Table

Differences are "Messages first" minus "Preferences first".

```{r}
#| label: Summary
slope_tbl <- as_tibble(slopes_order)
slope_p <- lrt_order$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]

summary_table <- bind_rows(
  rating_tests,
  reliability_table |> mutate(d = NA_real_),
  pref_tests,
  tibble(measure = "Preference straightlining (share)",
         prefs_first = prop.table(straight_table, 1)[order_levels[1], "TRUE"],
         messages_first = prop.table(straight_table, 1)[order_levels[2], "TRUE"],
         diff = messages_first - prefs_first,
         ci_low = NA_real_, ci_high = NA_real_, d = NA_real_,
         p = straight_test$p.value),
  agreement_test,
  tibble(measure = "Preference slope (rating per point of preference)",
         prefs_first = slope_tbl$pref_dev.trend[slope_tbl$pref_order == order_levels[1]],
         messages_first = slope_tbl$pref_dev.trend[slope_tbl$pref_order == order_levels[2]],
         diff = messages_first - prefs_first,
         # pairs() reports first level minus second, so flip the sign and the bounds
         ci_low = -slope_contrast$asymp.UCL, ci_high = -slope_contrast$asymp.LCL,
         d = NA_real_, p = slope_p)) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))

summary_table |>
  mutate(across(c(prefs_first, messages_first, diff, ci_low, ci_high, d), \(x) round(x, 3)),
         p = fmt_p(p), p_holm = fmt_p(p_holm)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

`p_holm` adjusts across the rows of this table. The two tone-specific tests
(order by tone on ratings and on preferences, and the three-way term in the
mixed model) are reported in their own sections.

# Notes and Caveats

-   **Preregistration.** The registered analysis for the secondary aim
    compares cross-validated model performance between the two halves. This
    memo's tests are more direct and more powerful but were not registered.
-   **Power.** With about 210 respondents per group, group differences smaller
    than roughly d = 0.27 will often be missed. A non-significant result here
    is weak evidence of no effect, not proof.
-   **What order cannot tell us.** Both groups rated the same messages, so
    this design shows whether exposure to examples changes stated
    preferences, not whether either set of preferences is "right".
-   **Context order.** `block_order_hi`, `block_order_hd` and `block_order_li`
    record the position of each risk context. They are not analyzed here but
    could be used to check for fatigue across the three rating blocks.
